FAP SYSTEM (Anti-Particle Filter)

INTRODUCTION

The FAP system (Anti-Particle Filter) is fitted on vehicles equipped with Diesel engines in order to reduce the particles present in the exhaust gases by more than 95%.

Particles comprise microspheres of carbon compounds, resulting from the imperfect combustion of the diesel fuel in the chamber. The particles cannot be eliminated through the use of regular catalytic converters, but through special filters known as anti-particle filters. The latter become unusable prematurely if used in urban cycles. The FAP. system allows the automatic regeneration of the anti-particle filter during the operation of the vehicle so that it remains efficient in all operating conditions for around 80,00 - 120,000 km (or 180,000 km starting from 12/2004) (depending on the version) after which the anti-particle filter should be replaced.

COMPOSITION

The FAP system consists of:

- a silicon carbide anti-particle filter in conjunction with a catalyzer (located upstream of the filter) and sensors for checking the temperature and pressure;

- a control logic integrated in the engine management node, designed to operate the artificial regeneration of the filter and guarantee the self-diagnosis of the system;

- an additive system which injects an appropriate amount of cerium oxide based additive (EOLYS DPX42 or EOLYS 176) into the fuel tank each time it is refilled. This additive lowers the combustion threshold for the particles from 550°C to 450°C.

ADDITIVE CONTROL NODE

The additive control node regulates the injection of additive into the fuel tank; the signals supplied by the following sensors are used for the management of this function:

- fuel level,

- fuel tank cap presence,

- engine speed,

- vehicle speed.

The fuel can be introduced either with the engine switched off or running.

Depending on the signals received, the additive control node, secured behind the dashboard, by the front passenger:

- determines the amount of additive to be injected,

- activates the additive injeciton pump,

- operates the additive injector.

The control logic includes:

- the management of the additive injection into the fuel tank,

- the calculation of the total quantity of additive injected from when the filter starts working,

- the recovery strategies,

- the diagnosis of the additive system, with the errors memorized,

- the exchange of information with both the engine management node and the body computer.

The additive control node also receives a signal from the exhaust gas temperature sensor (downstream of the filter) and sends it to the engine management node via the body computer.

ADDITIVE

The additive combines with the particles during combustion in order to:

- lower the combustion level of the particles by around 100°C,

- facilitate the propagation of the combustion of particle deposits.

The (EOLYS DPX42 or EOLYS 176) additive is a cerium oxide based compound diluted in a solvent and consists of:

- cerium oxide (about 4% mass),

- a product that allows the dilution of the oxide,

- solvent (combustible hydrocarbons).

During the combustion of the particles (which takes place in the anti-particle filter), the additive (cerium oxide) does not burn, but is deposited on the inner walls of the filter.

The additive injected into the fuel tank mixes spontaneously through the movement of the fuel in the actual tank.

MINIMUM LEVEL SENSOR

This sensor is incorporated in the pump assembly and is designed to notify the additive control node that the minimum level has been reached.

The sensor consists of a resistive element; the resistance value varies very quickly depending on whether it is immersed in the additive or exposed to the air (minimum level).

The minimum level is shown, starting from a quantity of additive equal to 0.3 litres, by the engine diagnostic warning light in the instrument panel coming on.

The quantity of additive corresponding to the reserve, guarantees six complete fuel refills; if the tank is refilled a greater number of times, the particle filter will become clogged and the engine management node will halt the regeneration strategies under these circumstances, at the same time restricting the fuel flow rate (limiting the vehicle speed).

SAFETY VALVE

The safety valve has the function of:

- insulating the tank from the introduction of dirt and water,

- regulating the pressure inside the tank as the level of the additive varies.

The valve consists of:

- vacuum valve (ensures that the correct pressure is maintained as the level of the additive decreases),

- pressure relief valve (guarantees that the excess pressure due to the evaporation of the solvent is discharged).

Opening the tank cap followed, at least 5 seconds later, by closing it, is known as a "cap cycle".

This cycle allows the additive node to understand that the fuel level is about to be altered.

ANTI-PARTICLE FILTER

The anti-particle filter is made from silicon carbide with a porous structure with channels that force the flow of exhaust gases through the walls. It is incorporated in the exhaust pipe fastened to the catalyzer.

The special structure of the filter allows:

- large filter capacity (up to 0.1 micron),

- loss of reduced load,

- good resistance to thermal, mechanical and chemical stresses,

- large storage capacity for particles which limits the regeneration frequency.

TEMPERATURE SENSOR DOWNSTREAM OF THE CATALYZER

This sensor allows the engine management node to monitor the temperature of the exhaust gases downstream of the catalytic converter and, as a result, the increase in temperature caused by the catalytic combustion.

DIFFERENTIAL PRESSURE SENSOR

The differential pressure sensor constantly measures the difference in pressure between the inlet and outlet of the catalytic converter/anti-particle filter assembly.

This measurement makes it possible to determine the blockage level of the filter. The sensor consists of:

- an electronic circuit for amplifying the signal,

- a sensitive diaphragm.

The diaphragm is subjected on one side to the catalytic converter inlet pressure (upstream) and on the other side to the filter oulet pressure (downstream).

The sensor provides a voltage proportional to the differential pressure measured by the diaphragm (?P = upstream pressure - downstream pressure).

The particles trapped on the filter walls, together with the additive and the other residues, naturally increase the loss of the load measured at the ends of the anti-particle filter during the course of its use.

PARTICLE FILTER CONTROL FUNCTION

The role of the control function is to:

- determine the state of the filter (blockage level),

- determine, if necessary, the activation of the regeneration aid function,

- check the efficiency of the artificial regeneration.

The following information is used by the engine management node in this area:

- distance travelled,

- differential pressure value,

- exhaust gas temperature downstream of the catalytic converter,

- exhaust gas temperature upstream of the catalytic converter,

- total quantity of additive injected,

- intake air flow rate.

Determining the filter blockage level

The total quantity of particles, cerium oxide and various residues present in the filter cause a variation in the load loss of the actual filter (the inlet pressure is different from the outlet pressure). This figure, constantly measured by the pressure sensor, represents the filter blockage level.

The engine management node map includes six different operating areas, determined starting from the calculation of the exhaust gas flow rate.

The exhaust gas flow rate is basically calculated using the following parameters:

- differential pressure,

- exhaust gas temperature downstream of the catalytic converter,

- intake air flow rate,

- atmospheric pressure.

The areas from "a" to "f" represent the different filter states calculated by the engine management node. Regeneration is designed to keep the filter within states "b" or "c" irrespective of the mileage covered or the driving style.

The engine management node activates the forced regeneration in the following cases:

- when the differential pressure values go from zone "c" to "d",

- when the differential pressure values entre zone "e",

- when the differential pressure values enter zone "c" and the driving conditions are favourable for regeneration (conditions in which regeneration will be faster).

Normal operating area from "b" to "d"

When moving from zone "c" towards zone "d" (more or less quickly depending on the driving conditions), the engine management node makes a request for regeneration aid to return the differential pressure values to within zone "b" or to zone "c" (depending on driving conditions).

Critical operating area: "e"

When regeneration is carried out in critical conditions or is interrupted, the quantity of particles stored by the filter is only partly destroyed. Under these circumstances the filter may become too clogged, the difference in pressure at the ends of the filter vary more rapidly; the engine management node detects that the filter is overloaded and signals this by switching on the diagnostic warning light in the instrument panel.

In these conditions the engine management node implements a reduced fuel flow rate strategy which, as a result, restricts the speed of the vehicle.

Abnormal operating areas: "a" and "f"

Zones "a" and "f" represent conditions in which the differential pressure is abnormal.

Zone "f" filter completely blocked: the differential pressure is constantly above 900 m/bar or above a level that varies according to the exhaust gas flow rate. In this condition the engine management node signals that the filter is overloaded by switching on the diagnostic warning light.

Zone "a" filter perforated: the differential pressure is below a certain level which is dependent on the flow rate. In this condition the engine management node signals that the filter is perforated by switching on the diagnostic warning light.

In these conditions the engine management node implements a reduced fuel flow rate strategy which, as a result, restricts the speed of the vehicle.

PARTICLE FILTER REGENERATION AID FUNCTION

Regeneration consists of periodically burning the particles accumulated in the filter, keeping it in the operating conditions identified by zone "b" (regenerated filter) or "c" (intermediate zone).

The role of the regeneration aid function is to:

- manage the control function requirements,

- acitvate the functions necessary for regeneration,

- determine the regeneration aid level needed,

- check the impact of post-injection on the operation of the engine.

The regeneration of the filter depends on the temperature of the exhaust gases and is activated beyond the particle combustion level (around 450°C if the additive function is present).

There are two types of regeneration:

- natural regeneration,

- artificial regeneration.

Natural regeneration

When the temperature of the exhaust gases approaches the regeneration level (with the additive function around 450 °C), the particles burn naturally inside the filter. In this case no intervention is required by the engine management node.

Driving conditions directly affect the temperature of the exhaust gases and, consequently, the temperature inside the filter.

Artificial regeneration

Artificial regeneration is managed by the engine management node by means of commands designed to increase the temperature of the exhaust gases until the particle combustion level is reached.

Artificial regeneration involves two stages:

- stage 1: increase in the temperature of the catalytic converter,

- stage 2: increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases.

The engine management node manages the change from the first stage to the second stage according to the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter; this change is not permitted until the first stage has been activated for a certain period or the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter have reached pre-set values.

Each time the artificial regeneration is activated, the engine management node:

- interrupts the exhaust gas recirculation (EGR);

- operates the turbine to keep the engine torque constant,

- if necessary, controls the opening of the valve for heating the intake air (through the reversal of the position of the two control valves),

- activates post-injection (which heats the exhaust gases directly),

- requests the activation of several electrical consumers.

Artificial regeneration - first stage

When first stage artificial regeneration is required, the engine management node adapts the post-injection strategies to increase the temperature of the catalytic converter.

Post-injection takes place immediately after the main injection which makes it possible to increase the temperature of the exhaust gases through combustion in the cylinder after top dead centre.

This stage ensures an increase in the temperature of the catalytic converter until the maximum efficiency level is reached.

By comparing the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter, the engine management node uses its internal strategy to determine whether the catalytic converter has reached its maximum conversion level; when this level is reached, it activates the second artificial regeneration stage.

Artificial regeneration - second stage

At the end of the first artificial regeneration stage, the engine management node implements strategies that allow a further increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases (second stage).

- the engine speed is equal to a pre-set level, artificial regeneration is inhibited during idling,

the vehicle has travelled at least 280 km since the last regeneration.

Counting the distance travelled

The information relating the distance travelled since the last regeneration (calculatd by the engine management node), makes it possible to activate the artificial regeneration independently of the information supplied by the differential pressure sensor. This strategy makes it possible to limit the mass of particles to be burnt by the filter since the combustion of a high level of particles could increase the temperature of the filter too much causing it to be ruined.

The engine managment node activates artificial regeneration strategies when the distance travelled since the last regeneration reaches a pre-set value, which varies according to the aging of the filter (quantity of cerium oxide accumulated).

"Economy" artificial regeneration

Artificial regeneration (mileage or differential pressure) can be activated in a way known as "economy".

The strategies remain unchanged compared with the previous description, but the injection times are shorter. This allows the regeneration of the filter with less fuel consumption.

This mode can be activated when the filter blockage level is not too high or when the mileage since the last regeneration is close to the limit. If conditions are favourable, the engine management node brings forward regeneration limiting fuel consumption for the actual regeneration.

The parameters required for activating this mode are:

- engine speed and load conditions favourable for rengeration for a set period (e.g. 80 km/h maintained for a period of more than 1 minute),

- N and ?P close to the values in the "economy" mode activation area.

Effects of the activation of artificial regeneration

During post-injection the fuel is injected after the piston has passed top dead centre. The temperature of the exhaust gases gradually increases until the regeneration level is reached.

The capacity, duration and time of the start of post-injection are determined by strategies that take the engine operating conditions and the level of assistance required into account.

Engine torque

When engine speed and load conditions are constant, post-injection produces an increase in engine torque. To maintain the same driving conditions and prevent a variation in engine torque, the engine management node:

- reduces the fuel flow rate during the main injection,

- modulates turbo pressure.

Reduction in the fuel flow rate during the main injection

The reduction in the fuel flow rate during the main injection makes it possible to cancel the increase in torque due to post-injection.

Regulation of supercharging pressure

In order to keep the engine torque unchanged during artificial regeneration, the engine management node reduces the supercharging pressure, restricting the flow of exhaust gases inside the turbine.

Activation of the high pressure pump third piston

During artificial regeneration the high pressure pump third piston is also activ ated to ensure the correct fuel flow rate required for post-injection.

Activation of electrical consumers

The activation of electrical consumers causes the engagement of the alternator and, as a result, an increase in resistant torque. This situation facilitates an increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases.

The engine management node request the body computer to switch on the electrical consumers that absorb a great deal of power, in the following order:

- the switching on of the heated rear windscreen,

- the switching on of the radiator cooling fan at low speed,

- the switching on of the radiator cooling fan at medium speed,

- the switching on of the heater plugs.

Regulation of the exhaust gas recirculation

Each time artificial regeneration is activated, the engine management node stops the exhaust gas recirculation (EGR): exhaust gas recirculation solenoid valve closed (this condition allows priority to be given to the management of the turbo).

Regulation of the intake air heating circuit

Each time artificial regeneration is activated, the engine management node heats the intake air in the cylinders, keeping the throttle valve on the air/water heater duct open and closing the one of the intercooler duct in order to force the flow of air inside the actual heater.

INTAKE AIR HEATING CIRCUIT

This device is designed to increase the temperature of the exhaust gases by increasing the temperature of the intake air, in order to facilitate the regeneration of the anti-particle filter (specific to the FAP device).

The device is only activated during the regeneration assistance stage and includes:

- an air/water heat exchanger;

- a throttle valve on the heater air inlet duct;

- an air/air heat exchanger;

AIR/WATER HEAT EXCHANGER (INTAKE AIR HEATING)

The water/air heat exchanger (1), installed near the air/air heat exchanger (intercooler), has the task of heating the intake air in the cylinders (during the particle filter regeneration assistance stage).

The intake air heater makes it possible to increase the temperature of the fuel required for the regeneration of the particle filter.

The NCM is operated by earthing the EGR solenoid valves and the intake air heater with a variable voltage.

Description

The air/air heat exchanger (intercooler) that cools the supercharging air, drawn into the cylinders, acts as a support for the water/air heat exchanger which has the task, in certain conditions, of heating the intake air.

The operation of the solenoid valve is the RCO type (cyclical opening ratio).

The proportional solenoid valve controlled with an RCO voltage is connected to the following elements:

- atmospheric pressure.

- vacuum supplied by the vacuum pump.

The pressure supplied by the solenoid lies between atmospheric pressure and vacuum pump vacuum level.

The solenoid valve places the vacuum pump and the heater valve in contact.

FAP REGENERATION ASSISTANCE OPERATING STAGES

During the heating stage:

- the EGR metering solenoid valve is controlled by being totally closed or it is not operated to return it to the rest position.

- the FAP heating solenoid valve is controlled when open or it is not operated to return it to the rest position (completely closed).
